For this purpose, we sampled 12 paleomagnetic sites representing six mineralized flow tops and their associated massive interiors on the Keweenaw Peninsula in Michigan. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: compo- nent. As this is not the case, hematization must have occurred before tectonic tilting to present attitudes. If the basalts were tilted to the southwest (away from the center of the rift) and opposite to their present-day tilt direction prior to hematiza- tion, the hematite component should be more steeply inclined, as is found in our study. We cannot eliminate this possibility completely, but geologic evidence strongly favors continuous, moderate tilting toward the present-day attitude during deposi- tion of the lavas and not in an opposite sense (White 1968). The steeper hematite components are probably not the result of apparent polar wander between basalt deposition and hema- tization, because the general movement between the primary and secondary components is perpendicular or opposite to the movement along the Keweenawan polar wander path (Fig. 7). The most likely explanation is that hematization occurred before any significant tilting or apparent polar wander. The primary magnetite component was acquired over a relatively short period of time when the lavas cooled and records a point on the secular variation curve. The secondary hematite compo- nent would have been acquired over a time span sufficiently long to average out a largeportion of the secular variation. h

f the Portage Lake Volcanics invites the opportunity to establish the relative age of copper mineralization. For this purpose, we sampled 12 paleomagnetic sites representing six mineralized flow tops and their associated massive interiors on the Keweenaw Peninsula in Michigan. Three of the four less- altered flow interiors contained two components of magnetization: one was canied by primary magnetite, and therefore the other, canied by hematite, must be secondary. The hematite component was parallel to the single hematite component in the associated flow top, indicating that both components had a common secondary origin. The low between-site dispersion of the hematite component and the similarity of the mean direction to primary directions of other rocks of the same age (1 100 Ma) suggest that hematization occurred over a period of time long enough to average out secular variation but before deposition of the overlying Nonesuch Shale, extensive tectonic tilting, and significant apparent polar wander. If the basalts were tilted to the southwest (away from the center of the rift) and opposite to their present-day tilt direction prior to hematiza- tion, the hematite component should be more steeply inclined, as is found in our study. We cannot eliminate this possibility completely, but geologic evidence strongly favors continuous, moderate tilting toward the present-day attitude during deposi- tion of the lavas and not in an opposite sense (White 1968). The steeper hematite components are probably not the result of apparent polar wander between basalt deposition and hema- tization, because the general movement between the primary and secondary components is perpendicular or opposite to the movement along the Keweenawan polar wander path (Fig. 7). The most likely explanation is that hematization occurred before any significant tilting or apparent polar wander. The primary magnetite component was acquired over a relatively short period of time when the lavas cooled and records a point on the secular variation curve. The secondary hematite compo- nent would have been acquired over a time span sufficiently long to average out a largeportion of the secular variation. h

Such a scatter can often be attributed to secondary components of magnetization superimposed upon the original magnetization after cooling. The older normal polarity and subsequent reversed polarity groups are found in lower Keweenawan rocks and have significantly different directions from the younger group with normal polarity which characterizes middle Keweenawan rocks. Received May 4, 1982 Revision accepted August 18, 1982 Two components of magnetization have been isolated from Chequamegon Sandstone samples using chemical demagnetization. A characteristic magnetization resides in magnetite of detrital origin. The pole calculated from this magnetization is 12.3"S, 177.7"E (K = 111.5, Ag5 = 4.6'). This pole lies with other poles of late Keweenawan age and is very close to the Jacobsville Sandstone poles. A secondary magnetization resides in authigenic hematite and yields a pole close to the present north pole. This high-latitude pole is known from an earlier study of the Chequamegon and has been used as evidence for the Hadrynian APW track. However, most if not all of the high-latitude poles that define the Hadrynian track are secondary and undated. Our preferred alternative to the Hadrynian track is that the high-latitude poles are recent remagnetizations and that the antipodal equatorial poles that mark its end points represent field reversals. Based on such a non-dipole model, Pesonen and Nevanlinna have offered a modified Logan Loop that is greatly reduced in 1 size from that originally proposed. The descending limb of the Logan Loop is defined by poles from middle and 1 upper Keweenawan volcanics and sediments. A critical link between the Keweenawan poles and the later Grenville poles is provided by secondary poles from the Middle River section (Orienta Formation) and the Fond du Lac Sandstone (Watts 1981). The Grenville poles, once considered as evidence for convergence between the Grenville Province and the North American craton, have been shown to represent magnetizations reset during the cooling of the Grenville Province (McWilliams and Dunlop 1975). Thus they postdate the orogenic event and must be considered cratonic North American poles. In addition to the well established Keweenawan and Grenville APW path segments, some poorly dated magnetizations, many demonstrably secondary, have been used to define an APW path termed the "Hadrynian track" (Morris and Roy 1977). Since the high-latitude poles that define these APW paths are undated, doubt must remain concerning their validity. Nevertheless, Piper (1981) used his North American APW path to propose a particular reconstruc- tion of a Late Precambrian supercontinent. The importance of such reconstructions in global tectonic studies warrants the close examination of the poles that at present define these APW paths. One critical high-latitude pole in both Hadrynian track models is the one derived from the Chequamegon Sandstone (DuBois 1962). DISCUSSION Magnetic Overprints Polyphase magnetization is the rule rather than the exception in these early Proterozoic formations. Detailed demagnetization studies are sometimes effective in isolating the various magnetic components but it is quite probable that many apparently aberrant data are caused by unresolved composite magnetizations. One effective way of investigating polyphase remanence is to consider the magnetic vectors removed during each step in incremental demagnetization runs. The results from the Stark and Tochatwi formations are aberrant, possibly because of a local tectonic rotation. This suggestion has been tested by collecting new material from the Stark Formation in an area thought to be undisturbed. Unfortunately, the strata there are brecciated and the specimens yield highly scattered directions which do not resolve the rotation problem. Since the samples were collected in ordered stratigraphic sequences it has proved possible to delineate geomagnetic polarity zones. The magnetostratigraphy of these ancient sedimentary basins is thus beginning to emerge, enabling certain tentative correlations between the various elements of the Coronation Geosyncline to be made. DISCUSSION Magnetic Overprints Polyphase magnetization is the rule rather than the exception in these early Proterozoic formations. Detailed demagnetization studies are sometimes effective in isolating the various magnetic components but it is quite probable that many apparently aberrant data are caused by unresolved composite magnetizations. One effective way of investigating polyphase remanence is to consider the magnetic vectors removed during each step in incremental demagnetization runs. This technique was developed in the early 1970s by E.W. McMurry and A.B. Reid at the University of Alberta and has become a widely accepted procedure in the last decade. It commonly enables one to recognize a recent (probably viscous remanent magnetization, VRM) magnetization acquired in the present ambient field and preferentially carried by grains of low blocking temp

The results from the Stark and Tochatwi formations are aberrant, possibly because of a local tectonic rotation. This suggestion has been tested by collecting new material from the Stark Formation in an area thought to be undisturbed. Unfortunately, the strata there are brecciated and the specimens yield highly scattered directions which do not resolve the rotation problem. Since the samples were collected in ordered stratigraphic sequences it has proved possible to delineate geomagnetic polarity zones. The magnetostratigraphy of these ancient sedimentary basins is thus beginning to emerge, enabling certain tentative correlations between the various elements of the Coronation Geosyncline to be made. The reference technique was the least-squares fitting of lines to segments of demagnetization trajectory (Kirschvink 1980). Minimum acceptance criteria adopted for this technique were: a minimum of four points on a line, with a maximum angular deviation of 7.5". Other techniques included least-squares fits to great-circle distributions (Halls 1976), and sequential vector subtractions. For these techniques, which only provided supporting evidence, the minimum acceptance criteria were, respectively: a minimum of four great-circle segments with arc lengths greater than 25", required to define an overprint component; and a maximum angular difference of 10" (determined by vector subtraction) between three sequentially subtracted vectors from the same specimen, the accepted direction being a vector mean of the three components. Site mean directions representative of the individual remanence components present at each site were calculated using the standard Fisher (1953) statistical techniques or the Kirschvink- derived (1980) specimen data directions. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: The Little Dal lavas were sampled at two localities separated by approximately 150 krn. From two sections through the lava sequence near the Keele River area (63"48'N, 231°30'E) 10 sites were obtained for paleomagnetic analysis. Six sites were sampled at a second locality near Coates Lake in the Thundercloud Range (62"24'N, 233"4OtE). At each site at least six 2 in. (5 cm) cores were collected by field drilling. Two specimens were sliced from each core. The bedding orientation at each sampling locality was measured on the nearest sedimentary unit. The difference in structural orientation between the two areas provided a possible fold test of remanence age. At the Keele River sites the beds dip moderately to the west, and at the Coates Lake sites the beds dip steeply to the east. As this folding was probably developed during the Mesozoic orogeny, the fold test does not provide a precise age control of the magnetization; magnetizations passing a positive fold test are merely constrained to the interval Late Precambrian through Cretaceous. Carey @. 191) defined curved orogenic belts as oro- clines, that is, "orogenic belt[s] with a change in trend which is interpreted as an impressed strain."

Noms and Larochelle in 1966 attempted to use paleomag- netism to test whether the Mackenzie Arc was an orocline by studying Late Proterozoic (770 Ma; Armstrong et al. 1982) diabase sills and dykes from around the arc. However, the then-current laboratory methods and the absence of compara- tive paleomagnetic data from the region precluded interpreta- tion of the results. The sample collection and initial data were later given to the senior author, and after additional experi- ments were performed, notably thermal demagnetization, the results were combined with those from another paleomagnetic I study of Mackenzie Mountains diabases (Park 1981). Collec- tively, the data imply that the arcuate shape of the orogenic 1 belt is essentially, if not wholly, primary in nature. It is not orocline. Earth Sci. 26, 2194-2203 (1989) Introduction Curved orogenic belts have been explained as either primary (Wilson 1954) or secondary (Carey 1958) megascopic struc- tures, inheriting their curvature either from the original shape of the craton margin or from later dynamic bending of the margin. Carey @. 191) defined curved orogenic belts as oro- clines, that is, "orogenic belt[s] with a change in trend which is interpreted as an impressed strain."

Noms and Larochelle in 1966 attempted to use paleomag- netism to test whether the Mackenzie Arc was an orocline by studying Late Proterozoic (770 Ma; Armstrong et al. 1982) diabase sills and dykes from around the arc. However, the then-current laboratory methods and the absence of compara- tive paleomagnetic data from the region precluded interpreta- tion of the results. The sample collection and initial data were later given to the senior author, and after additional experi- ments were performed, notably thermal demagnetization, the results were combined with those from another paleomagnetic I study of Mackenzie Mountains diabases (Park 1981). Ilmenite, occumng as trellis, sandwich, or composite struc- tures or in myrmekitic intergrowths, is generally pristine, but it may be partly or wholly altered to leucoxene in several sites in northwestern British Columbia. In general, even rather fresh looking magnetite has altered to several microcrystalline phases, which are not readily identifiable. In its most altered state magnetite appears to have been either replaced or com- pletely dissolved, leaving a network of ilmenite laths. The microgranular phases of the least-altered grains probably include maghemite and hematite, evidence for which was dis- cussed in Park (1981). Additional opaque minerals include sulfides, commonly associated with the ilmenite-magnetite grains. Carriers of the magnetization Primary magnetization resolved in the previous diabase study was thought to occur as both normal and reverse remanences in maghemite (AR, AN) and hematite (BR, BN) (Park 1981). A third carrier, magnetite, was considered as con- taining part of an unresolved magnetization RM, thought to be composed of antiparallel remanences with the AR - BR and AN-BN directions. In the present study there are normal and reverse remanence directions that have the magnetite blocking- temperature range (Figs. 3c, 3d, 4a, 4b), thus supporting the previous conjecture on the nature of much of the mixed RM magnetization (Park 1981). The periodic field-reversal hypothesis in its modern form, with the last reversal ending in early Quaternary time, was first proposed by Matuyama (1929, p. 205). Each grain of magnetic material in a rock consists of one or more magnetic domains, and although the directions of magnetization are different in different domains, the intensity of magnetization per unit volume, termed the spontaneous magnetization J$, is the same in all domains of the same mineral. All paleomagnetic measurements available to the authors are here compiled and eval- uated, with a key to the summary table and illustrations in English and Russian. The principles upon which the evaluation of paleomagnetic measurements is based are sum- marized, with special emphasis on statistical methods and on the evidence and tests for magnetic stability and paleomagnetic applicability. Evaluation of the data summarized leads to the following general conclusions: (1) The earth's average magnetic field, throughout Oligocene to Recent time, has very closely approximated that due to a dipole at the center of the earth orientetl parallel to the present axis of rotation. Sampling Procedure and Measurements In the present paleomagnetic study, 40 oriented block samples from the Pon- tgrave and Becancour Formations were collected at 8 sites on unaltered outcrops where the stratigraphic relations and the structures are well known. Site 1 is . located on the bank of Gentilly river, sites 2, 3 and 4 on the banks of Becancour river, site 5 on the bank of Orignaux river, sites 6 and 7 on the banks of Chene river and site 10 on the bank of Nicolet river. Five sites (2, 3, 4, 7 and 10) are within the Becancour Formation and the three others (1, 5 and 6) within the Pontgrave Formation (Fig. 1). Magnetization was measured with a digital spinner magnetometer (DSM-1). Two methods of demagnetization were carried out using (1) an AF demagnetizer with three-axis tumbler operating in residual fields of about 5 nT (SEGUIN, 1975) and (2) a field-free electrical oven (SEGUIN, 1973/74) and a Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer (STD-1) with residual fields less than 15 nT. Stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal procedures were used up to 100 mT and 660℃, respectively. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each oriented core sample was obtained from the mean of at least two specimens(diameter 2.5 cm, height 2.2 cm). Single measurements of NRM were usually repeated to within 4% in intensity (J) and within 3° in direction (declination D, inclination I). 4.

Sampling Procedure and Measurements In the present paleomagnetic study, 40 oriented block samples from the Pon- tgrave and Becancour Formations were collected at 8 sites on unaltered outcrops where the stratigraphic relations and the structures are well known. Site 1 is . located on the bank of Gentilly river, sites 2, 3 and 4 on the banks of Becancour river, site 5 on the bank of Orignaux river, sites 6 and 7 on the banks of Chene river and site 10 on the bank of Nicolet river. Five sites (2, 3, 4, 7 and 10) are within the Becancour Formation and the three others (1, 5 and 6) within the Pontgrave Formation (Fig. 1). Magnetization was measured with a digital spinner magnetometer (DSM-1). Two methods of demagnetization were carried out using (1) an AF demagnetizer with three-axis tumbler operating in residual fields of about 5 nT (SEGUIN, 1975) and (2) a field-free electrical oven (SEGUIN, 1973/74) and a Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer (STD-1) with residual fields less than 15 nT. Stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal procedures were used up to 100 mT and 660℃, respectively. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each oriented core sample was obtained from the mean of at least two specimens(diameter 2.5 cm, height 2.2 cm). Single measurements of NRM were usually repeated to within 4% in intensity (J) and within 3° in direction (declination D, inclination I). 4.

Conclusions (1) A suite of Carboniferous dykes from the Sandwich Bay area of coastal Labrador is recognized as distinct from other dykes in the area based on their geochemistry - field character- istics and their paleomagnetic behaviour. (2) The dykes are chemically homogeneous and are con- sidered within-plate tholeiites. (3) A K- Ar whole-rock age of 327 k 13 Ma was deter- mined for a member of this suite of dykes and was interpreted as the age of intrusion of the Sandwich Bay dykes. (4) Paleomagnetic signature of the dykes is uncomplicated, constituting a PEF component superposed on a characteristic magnetization that is northwest and upward directed. None of the dykes has a Kiaman overprint. Baked-contact tests for various dykes in the group are positive, suggesting that the isolated stable remanence of the dykes is primary. (5) The paleopole position for this suite of dykes is at 16.2"N, 157.6"E, which is interpreted as representative of the paleomagnetic field 327 Ma ago. The corresponding paleolati- 2290 CAN. J. This was attributed to the presence of two thermally stable magnetizations acquired, one before and one after, a field reversal, and it was concluded that much of the information contained in those red beds could not be obtained from thermal experiments alone. If so, then red beds are a valuable source of information for the study of certain features (e.g., field reversals) of the earth's field in the past. However, the problem is to extract that information, and the pre- liminary experiments indicate that in order to do so a special procedure is needed. Those re- sults show that only chemical leaching can isolate one (the DRM) of the three magneti- zations. The two cleaning techniques complement each other, and it appears that an analysis of com- bined thermal and chemical results might pro- vide much of the information contained in red beds. DOLERITE SILL AND REMAGNETIZED ESAYOO BASALT A dolerite sill 105 m in thickness was sampled at site 20. It has a simple magnetization. AF dema~etization yields consistent directions which become inter- nally random above 80 mT (Fig. 7). Thermal demagnetization yields a near-perfect square-shouldered curve with unblocking temperatures between 500” and 575°C with random directions above that temperature (Fig. 8). Polished sections of the dolerite show large grains of magnetite (200 pm) with ilmenite lamella. After cleaning, all specimens have a well-grouped, near-vertical, downward direction, as would be expected for Cretaceous rocks (Fig. 9, Table I). Samples of Esayoo basalt were also obtained at a distance of 30 m strati~aphically below the sill. Single component magnetizations only were found but the directions are similar to those of the sill and quite different from the Esayoo at greater distances. This is born out by studies of polished sections from each site. Hematite is ubiquitous both as disseminated crystals, generally elongated ranging up to 100 pm and down to less than 1 pm in length, and as rims and fracture-fillings of olivine and pyroxene crystals. Only in two sections small (10 pm) discrete grains of magnetite were observed after a considerable search; it is a rare mineral in these rocks. Hence although magnetite could carry some of the remanence, hematite is the main source and the spread in unblocking temperatures is presumably caused by the presence in it of variable amounts of impurities (probably ilmenite) and by the wide range of grain-sizes present. The Esayoo Formation (Lower Permian) of northern Ellesmere Island (81°N, 82’W) has been sampled at two localities (twelve sites, 88 cores studied) in the Early Tertiary (Eurekan orogeny) fold and thrust belt of the northern Sverdrup Basin, northern Ellesmere Island. The directions of remanent magnetization at the two localities are in excellent agreement after correction for geological tilt. Their mean is 126.2”, - 61.8’ (3 (sites) = 12, k = 105, czas = 4.3O) and the corresponding paleopole is 48.1 “N, 159.2”E (K = 52, A,, = 6.1”). Comparison with Early Permian reference paleopoles for North America shows that the formation of overthrust sheets has produced no pal~magnetically detectable displacement in a paleolatitudinal sense as would be inferred from the geology, but there is a significant anticlockwise rotation of 36*8’. This rotation is the first to be observed in the Canadian Arctic Islands. Geological evidence allows no more than about 50 km of lateral motion along Nares Strait between Ellesmere Island and Greenland. This falls far short of the 300 km of

trait between Ellesmere Island and Greenland. This falls far short of the 300 km of relative motion required by the marine geophysical evidence for the opening of the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay. This discrepancy between the geological and geophysical evidence is the Nares Strait paradox. Evidently relative motion between Greenland and Ellesmere Island is not restricted to Nares Strait itself and must be more generaBy distributed across Eltesmere Island. We suggest that the 36” rotation observed is a manifestation of this distributed strain, and therefore provides a clue to the solution of the Nares Strait paradox. It is unlikely, therefore, that the HT1 magnetization records a reversal of the geomagnetic field that occurred as the lavas initially cooled. As we describe below, the overlying tuffs have directions similar to HT1. The lower Fundy Group red beds of the Wolfville and lower Blomidon formations in Nova Scotia and of Wolfville-equivalent units in New Brunswick are exposed around the Bay of Fundy. These red beds were sampled at twenty-six shoreline sites for paleomagnetic analysis, primarily by thermal step demagnetization methods. Samples from four sites proved too fragile to core; however, coating many of the rest of these poorly-indurated samples and cores with waterglass enabled them to withstand the rigours of coring, measurement and thermal cleaning. A stable hematite remanence was found in all twenty-one coherent sites with normal, reversed and mixed polarities. Con- glomerate and fold tests indicate the remanence is either primary or very early diagenetic. The lower Fundy Group red beds of the Wolfville and lower Blomidon formations in Nova Scotia and of Wolfville-equivalent units in New Brunswick are exposed around the Bay of Fundy. These red beds were sampled at twenty-six shoreline sites for paleomagnetic analysis, primarily by thermal step demagnetization methods. Samples from four sites proved too fragile to core; however, coating many of the rest of these poorly-indurated samples and cores with waterglass enabled them to withstand the rigours of coring, measurement and thermal cleaning. A stable hematite remanence was found in all twenty-one coherent sites with normal, reversed and mixed polarities. Con- glomerate and fold tests indicate the remanence is either primary or very early diagenetic. Its mean direction is D = 196S0, I= -3.8O (ag5= 7.2O) which converts to a pole position of 45.3ON, 97.1°E (dp = 3.6O. dm = 7.2O). This pole indicates that the lower Fundy Group was likely deposited in the Early Triassic, rather than in the Middle and Late Triassic, as currently thought. It also indicates that the Nova Scotia platform was rotated about 8’ clockwise after deposition of the lower Fundy Group and before extrusion of the North Mountain basalts. Most of the magnetizations from site 03 are B or C type (10 out of 12 specimens). The specimen from site 14 (basalt) exhibits typical single-domain grain behaviour, the low-field TRM being more stable than the saturation IRM. Except for two specimens with magnetizations that are directed toward the west and associated with lightning strikes, the NRM's from site 14 show a good cluster because the original TRM is very stable. Specimens from site 14 show mainly A-type mag- netizations (7 out of 9 specimens). Therefore A- and C-type magnetizations are related to single-domain- and multi- domain-behaviour magnetic carriers, respectively. B-type magnetizations are probably related to magnetic carriers showing intermediate behaviour. The coastal flexure in E Greenland is a seaward facing monocline which marks the present coastline for some 600 km between approximately 66 and 70"N (Fig. 1). To the NE of Kangerdlugssuaq, along the Blosseville Kyst, the flexure affects Palaeogene basalts. On the outer headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. Soper SUMMARY: The well known coastal flexure of central E Greenland, with its associated dyke swarm, affects a thick pile of Tertiary basalts and the underlying basement gneisses. It is a major tectonic/magmatic feature of this 'trailing edge' type continental margin. The original interpretation of Wager & Deer (1938) envisaged the emplacement of the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm in the convex arc of the flexure. Nielsen (1975, 1978) recognized several episodes of dyke emplacement. He interpreted the main swarm (THOL 1) as earlier than the flexure, emplaced vertically into the horizontal basalt pile and subsequently tilted by antithetic faulting during the formation of the flexure. A palaeomagnetic study of the THOL 1 and later dykes shows that the former were emplaced in their present inclined attitude. This discriminates in favour of Wager's interpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. (b) Several authors (Johnson, Murphy & Torreson 1948; King 1955; King & Rees 1966; Blow & Hamilton 1978) have shown that artificially deposited sediments often preserve an inclination significantly shallower than that of the ambient field. Discrepancies in excess of 20" are quite possible and thus the relatively small polar offset found in the present study (14" for the complete dataset, 11" if the perturbations are excluded) could well be due to such a sedimentological cause. However there is a growing body of evidence (Barton & McElhinny 1979; Tucker 1983) that real sediments actually carry a post-depositional remanence (PDRM) which enables grain re-adjustment in water-filled voids such that the inclination discrepancy is greatly reduced or even entirely removed. three major sedimentary basins in the northern Yukon, which itself is part of a much broader region stretching eastwards from the Bering Straits to the Richardson Mountains, and southwards from the Beaufort Sea to Whitehorse. Even during periods of advanced glaciation this region - often referred to as Beringia - remained unglaciated and therefore served as a refuge for plants and animals, possibly including the first human beings in North America. Fuller accounts of the archeological, geological, and geomorphological details can be found in papers by Hughes (1969, 1972) and Morlan (1980). Certain studies have shown that partial correction for bedding attitudes produces acceptable dispersions (Schwartz and van der Voo 1984), as if magnetizations were acquired at a certain stage during the deformation process, perhaps even controlled by it. This is unlikely to be generally true because many different combinations of primary, syndeformational, and postdeformational magnetization may ~ be expected to occur within single rock units. For example, one recent study has revealed magnetizations acquired before and during defor- mation, evidently by two quite different processes, because the two magnetizations had different unblocking temperatures (Miller and Kent 1986). Rocks may be expected to acquire their magnetization at deposition or during diagenesis by a variety of thermal and chemical processes, and it is the variety of these processes and their temporal relationship to deformation that creates the difficulty in determining the paleomagnetic horizontal. In the first part of this paper we describe the magnetization of a vol- canic sequence in the vicinity of Kelowna, British Columbia. Above the OVF, the hanging wall is composed of low-grade late Paleozoic and Mesozoic eugeosynclincal rocks cut by Jurassic plutons. K-Ar mica dates of Jurassic age (Medford 1975) are preserved in the plutons, indicating that they, and the hanging- wall rocks, have not been heated above 300°C since emplace- ment. In contrast, K - Ar dates from micas and hornblende and fission-track dates on apatite and sphene from footwall gneisses of the OVF indicate that they were heated to a tem- perature above 500°C until 52 Ma, and then cooled rapidly to 100°C within about 5 Ma (Medford 1975; Parkinson 1985; Mathews 1981). Such metamorphic rocks might be expected to preserve a record of the middle Eocene geomagnetic field. The sampling region in the vicinity of Kelowna is shown in Fig. 3. The volcanics are accessible by road and are exposed in long semicontinuous sections, capped by late middle Eocene lacustrine sedimentary rocks, which provide excellent deter- minations of bedding attitude. Petrographic observations of the kimberlites in this study are generally consistent with Mitchell's [1986] review. Apart from ilmenite, the micropheno- crystic oxide grains, when present, are invariably zoned from gray magnesium-aluminum- chrome-rich cores toward browner, more ulvospinel-rich borders. The bulk of the very fine-grained matrix spinels are homogeneous, resembling the outer rims of the zoned microphenocrysts. In size, matrix spinel particles decrease to below the limit of microscopic resolution (1-10 m). Whether these smallest grains are the product of primary crystallization or are by-products of subsolidus serpentinization or carbonation is not clear. But in either case, they would trend in composition toward purer magnetite [Mitchell, 1986]. Increasing substitution of Mg, A1, Cr, and Ti in magnetite is known to lower the Curie point markedly and progressively [Nishitani, 1981; Schmidbauer, 1983]. Kumar and Bhalla [1984] studied a natural chromite ore and found that it carried a remanance with a blocking temperature of -350øC. Thus given the composition spectrum of spinel microphenocrysts in kimberlites, they may carry a pure thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) even in diatreme-facies whose temperatures of emplacement may be as low as -350øC (see below). Subordinate sampling was also undertaken in a younger hornblende dacite intrusion (=35 Ma) and the overlying tuff of North Creek (---35 Ma). In general, ash flow tuffs cool and are magnetized within a short period of time relative to geomagnetic secular variation and their eutaxitic structures typically indicate the paleohorizontal. tween-site vertical axis rotations and thus the relative importance of strike-slip faulting to the mechanism of extension. Subordinate sampling was also undertaken in a younger hornblende dacite intrusion (=35 Ma) and the overlying tuff of North Creek (---35 Ma). In general, ash flow tuffs cool and are magnetized within a short period of time relative to geomagnetic secular variation and their eutaxitic structures typically indicate the paleohorizontal. These attributes of ash flow tuffs, in addition to their generally widespread occurrence, make them excellent candidates for combined paleomagnetic and structural studies of regional deformation. However, in this study a number of problems associated with the paleomagnetism of the Kalamazoo Tuff are documented; they include topography-related variations of the eutaxitic structures, secular variation during slow cooling, postblocking rheomorphic flow, and local remagnetization of the tuff by younger igneous activity. The tilt-corrected data, with these sources of error reduced or eliminated, exhibit a 28 ø -+ 12 ø clockwise rotation of the Schell Creek Range relative to the Kern Mountains region. This rotation implies differential extension accommo- dated by strike-slip faulting or N-S shortening. The paleomagnetic results also

es of regional deformation. However, in this study a number of problems associated with the paleomagnetism of the Kalamazoo Tuff are documented; they include topography-related variations of the eutaxitic structures, secular variation during slow cooling, postblocking rheomorphic flow, and local remagnetization of the tuff by younger igneous activity. The tilt-corrected data, with these sources of error reduced or eliminated, exhibit a 28 ø -+ 12 ø clockwise rotation of the Schell Creek Range relative to the Kern Mountains region. This rotation implies differential extension accommo- dated by strike-slip faulting or N-S shortening. The paleomagnetic results also suggest that large changes in strike of layered units near faults with presumed strike-slip movement need not be the result of oroclinal bending, but could result from superimposed sets of orthogonal normal faults. INTRODUCTION Exposed in the hills and mountain ranges of east central Nevada are rocks that were involved in an intense episode of crustal extension in middle Tertiary time. The extension is characterized by a subhorizontal detachment fault above which supracrustal rocks have been thinned by brittle defor- mation and below which midcrustal igneous and metamor- phic rocks have been ductilely deformed [e.g., Coney, 1

vada [Hudson and Geissman, 1987] which imply that locally, regions of extension are associated with strike-slip faults as well as normal faults. In eastern Nevada, north-south vari- ations in the magnitude and direction of tilting and the discontinuous nature of many of the major fault systems suggest that the extensional strain was heterogeneous and that strike-slip faults played a significant role in the exten- sion. Large changes in the strike of layered rocks near faults with apparent strike-slip displacement suggest that in places vertical axis rotations may have been large (as much as 90ø). A paleomagnetic study of crustal deformation in the vicinity of the Las Vegas Valley Shear Zone by Nelson and Jones [1987] also has documented large rotations of relatively small blocks and has shown that in this region the crust can be modeled as a thin non-Newtonian viscous plate. Similarly, documentation of vertical axis rotations within the highly extended zone of east central Nevada, could assess the role of strike-slip faulting and provide important constraints on the geometry, kinematics, and lateral heterogeneity of ex- tension within the brittle crust. Subordinate sampling was also undertaken in a younger hornblende dacite intrusion (=35 Ma) and the overlying tuff of North Creek (---35 Ma). tween-site vertical axis rotations and thus the relative importance of strike-slip faulting to the mechanism of extension. Subordinate sampling was also undertaken in a younger hornblende dacite intrusion (=35 Ma) and the overlying tuff of North Creek (---35 Ma). In general, ash flow tuffs cool and are magnetized within a short period of time relative to geomagnetic secular variation and their eutaxitic structures typically indicate the paleohorizontal. These attributes of ash flow tuffs, in addition to their generally widespread occurrence, make them excellent candidates for combined paleomagnetic and structural studies of regional deformation. However, in this study a number of problems associated with the paleomagnetism of the Kalamazoo Tuff are documented; they include topography-related variations of the eutaxitic structures, secular variation during slow cooling, postblocking rheomorphic flow, and local remagnetization of the tuff by younger igneous activity. The tilt-corrected data, with these sources of error reduced or eliminated, exhibit a 28 ø -+ 12 ø clockwise rotation of the Schell Creek Range relative to the Kern Mountains region. This rotation implies differential extension accommo- dated by strike-slip faulting or N-S shortening. The paleomagnetic results also

es of regional deformation. However, in this study a number of problems associated with the paleomagnetism of the Kalamazoo Tuff are documented; they include topography-related variations of the eutaxitic structures, secular variation during slow cooling, postblocking rheomorphic flow, and local remagnetization of the tuff by younger igneous activity. The tilt-corrected data, with these sources of error reduced or eliminated, exhibit a 28 ø -+ 12 ø clockwise rotation of the Schell Creek Range relative to the Kern Mountains region. This rotation implies differential extension accommo- dated by strike-slip faulting or N-S shortening. The paleomagnetic results also suggest that large changes in strike of layered units near faults with presumed strike-slip movement need not be the result of oroclinal bending, but could result from superimposed sets of orthogonal normal faults. INTRODUCTION Exposed in the hills and mountain ranges of east central Nevada are rocks that were involved in an intense episode of crustal extension in middle Tertiary time. The extension is characterized by a subhorizontal detachment fault above which supracrustal rocks have been thinned by brittle defor- mation and below which midcrustal igneous and metamor- phic rocks have been ductilely deformed [e.g., Coney, 1

nge-by-range palinspastic re- constructions and restoration of older Mesozoic structures indicate that the magnitude of extension averages approxi- mately 250% or 95 km across this zone [Gans and Miller, 19831. The major objective of this study is to assess, using paleomagnetic data, the role of vertical axis rotations within the highly extended region of eastern Nevada. Rotations of fault blocks around near-vertical axes are a likely conse- quence of crustal extension within domains of strike-slip faults [e.g., Ron et al., 1984]. Although strike-slip faulting is considered subordinate to normal faulting in the overall Cenozoic deformation of the Basin and Range province, paleomagnetic studies have determined block rotations near Copyright 1989 by the American Geophysical Union. tween-site vertical axis rotations and thus the relative importance of strike-slip faulting to the mechanism of extension. Subordinate sampling was also undertaken in a younger hornblende dacite intrusion (=35 Ma) and the overlying tuff of North Creek (---35 Ma). In general, ash flow tuffs cool and are magnetized within a short period of time relative to geomagnetic secular variation and their eutaxitic structures typically indicate the paleohorizontal. These attributes of ash flow tuffs, in addition to their generally widespread occurrence, make them excellent candidates for combined paleomagnetic and structural studies of regional deformation. However, in this study a number of problems associated with the paleomagnetism of the Kalamazoo Tuff are documented; they include topography-related variations of the eutaxitic structures, secular variation during slow cooling, postblocking rheomorphic flow, and local remagnetization of the tuff by younger igneous activity. The tilt-corrected data, with these sources of error reduced or eliminated, exhibit a 28 ø -+ 12 ø clockwise rotation of the Schell Creek Range relative to the Kern Mountains region. Kent Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory and Department of Geological Sciences, Columbia University, Palisades, New York Abstract. Two components of magnetization were isolated in the Upper Ordovician Juniata Formation sampled in the area of the Pennsylvania salient. The thermally distributed, reversed polarity B component was most likely acquired during Alleghenian deformation, and although it is poorly grouped, it is similar to other Appalachian synfolding magnetizations. The pre-Alleghenian age C magnetization is entirely of normal polarity and shows a difference in declinations between the mean magnetizations isolated on the northern and southern limbs of the salient of 24° ± 23°. This anomaly is consistent with the sense and magnitude of declination anomalies observed in pre-Alleghenian magnetizations isolated in other throughgoing Appalachian red beds of Silurian, Devonian, and early Carboniferous age. The mean inclination of -44.7° suggests a paleolatitude of about 26°S for the central Appalachians in the Late Ordovician. This paleolatitude fits a trend of southward motion of North America from the Ordovician to the Early Devonian, followed by northward drift thr

This sediment package was deformed in the Permo-Carboniferous Alleghenian orogeny [Dennison, 1982]. The relatively simple structure of the Valley and Ridge Province and the easily measured, high stability magnetizations of the red beds made these rocks prime candidates for paleomagnetic study. Indeed, these units were some of the first rocks to be sampled for paleomagnetic study in North America, with one of the first positive fold tests having been recorded in samples taken from the Rose Hill by Graham [1949]. The Juniata red beds were first sampled for paleomagnetic study some 30 years ago [Collinson and Runcorn, 1960]. Data from this early study were used to help bolster the first-order observation of continental drift between North America and Europe. These original data represented the total natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the samples as no demagnetization was done on the collection. The B components from both the northern and southern limbs of the salient are poorly grouped with a maximum precision parameter (k) value for the northern sites of 11.5 and only 8.2 for the southern sites. The north limb B component is best grouped at 50% tilt correction with a mean declination/inclination of 180.0°/-5.0° (a95 = 28.3, for N = 4 sites; Table 1). The south limb B component obtains its best grouping at 80% tilt correction with a mean direction of 174.4°/-5.9° (a95 = 19.2° for N = 9 sites). No fold test was possible for the sites from the hinge zone, as the two sites which had interpretable magnetizations shared a common strike and dip. The revised results from the Mauch Chunk and Catskill, as well as new data from the Bloomsburg Formation [Kent, 1988], reveal a declination anomaly in the pre-Alleghenian age magnetizations between the northern and southern limbs of the Pennsylvania salient which could indicate oroclinal rotation. In addition, the recent results from the Lower Devonian Andreas red beds [Miller and Kent, 1988a] and from the Bloomsburg [Kent, 1988] both show a best grouping of the highest stability component at less than full tilt correction, perhaps indicative of some remagnetization and folding associated with the Devonian Acadian orogeny even though structural evidence for Acadian deformation in the central Appalachians is ambiguous. The major Paleozoic Appalachian red beds which have not been restudied since the recognition of synfolding Kiaman remagnetizations are the Juniata, Rose Hill, and Dunkard formations. The purpose of the current study is to report new results for the Juniata. In the study of Vander Voo and French [1977], the Juniata was sampled primarily in the southern limb of the Pennsylvania salient. Kent Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory and Department of Geological Sciences, Columbia University, Palisades, New York Abstract. Two components of magnetization were isolated in the Upper Ordovician Juniata Formation sampled in the area of the Pennsylvania salient. The thermally distributed, reversed polarity B component was most likely acquired during Alleghenian deformation, and although it is poorly grouped, it is similar to other Appalachian synfolding magnetizations. The pre-Alleghenian age C magnetization is entirely of normal polarity and shows a difference in declinations between the mean magnetizations isolated on the northern and southern limbs of the salient of 24° ± 23°. The mean inclination of -44.7° suggests a paleolatitude of about 26°S for the central Appalachians in the Late Ordovician. The interval between eruption of the Pahute Mesa and Trail Ridge members was too brief for reestablishment of chemical stratification in the Black Mountain magma system. Nevertheless, a small volume of highly evolved comendite magma developed and was erupted as lava within the Black Mountain caldera and as a component of the Trail Ridge Member. The short repose interval and rapid development of the comendite, together with evidence for mixing of magmas of silicic to near-mafic composition (Vogel et al., this issue), and the presence of air-fall tuff at the base of the Trail Ridge, lead us to conclude that eruption of the Trail Ridge Member was probably triggered by injection of hot, relatively unevolved magma into the Black Mountain magma body. Published paleomagnetic data from Cretaceous plutons (for example, the Coast Plutonic Complex) intruding the thrust belt suggest that it has been displaced northward by as much as 2400 km since 90-100 Ma. This study focuses on the preintrusive travel history of the Decatur terrane, one of the units involved in the San Juan thrusting. The Decatur terrane is of special interest because it may be correlative with the Coast Range ophiolite (CRO) and Great Valley sequence of the southern California Coast Ranges. However, preliminary results of along-strike trends in the Appalachian remagnetization age [Miller and Kent, 1988] suggest that remagnetization occurred somewhat earlier in the southern Ap- palachians than the northern Appalachians, in accord with the ob- served south to north progression of Alleghenian deformation. In another study, variations in magnetite concentration in Devonian limestones in an east-west transect across New York State [Jackson et al., 1988b] were found to be strongly covariant with differences in the degree of diagenetic illitization within a Devo- nian bentonire horizon. It was inferred that illitization and mag- netite authigenesis were controlled by the same diagenetic factors and that both occurred during the late Paleozoic, in accord with a chemical remagnetization model. The results of these inves- tigations indicate that additional regional studies will further in- crease our understanding of these remagnetizations, their geologic context, and their causes

State University, Baton Rouge We report paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from sedimentary carbonates of the Appalachian Basin that have implications for the mechanism of widespread late Paleozoic remagnetization in this rock type. Sampling was accomplished mostly along two across-basin transects, one in Devonian carbonates of New York State and the other in Ordovician and Mississippian carbonates of Tennessee and Alabama. Paleomagnetic investigations of the New York Devonian carbonates along a transect from Albany to Buffalo indicate that these rocks were completely remagnetized in Alleghenian time. Rock magnetic studies show that magnetite concentration varies in a regular fashion along the transect with a local maximum near Syracuse and decreasing gradually to the east and west. This pattem shows a striking correlation with the degree of diagenetic alteration of clay minerals in a Devonian bentonire horizon which took place during Alleghenian time. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: BARB ARAS AFFER Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge We report paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from sedimentary carbonates of the Appalachian Basin that have implications for the mechanism of widespread late Paleozoic remagnetization in this rock type. Sampling was accomplished mostly along two across-basin transects, one in Devonian carbonates of New York State and the other in Ordovician and Mississippian carbonates of Tennessee and Alabama. Paleomagnetic investigations of the New York Devonian carbonates along a transect from Albany to Buffalo indicate that these rocks were completely remagnetized in Alleghenian time. Rock magnetic studies show that magnetite concentration varies in a regular fashion along the transect with a local maximum near Syracuse and decreasing gradually to the east and west. This pattem shows a striking correlation with the degree of diagenetic alteration of clay minerals in a Devonian bentonire horizon which took place during Alleghenian time. We conclude that most of the magnetite present in these carbonates is of authigenic origin and that clay mineral alteration and magnetite authigenesis were coeval, late Paleozoic events that were controlled by the same diagenetic factors. Paleomagnetic studies indicate that late Paleozoic re- magnetization has affected Ordovician carbonates of the Nashville Dome. Paleozoic carbonates in the overthrust belt near Chattanooga also carry the late Paleozoic remagnetization. However, Mississippian carbonates between the dome and the overthrust belt are very weakly magnetized and show no evidence for late Paleozoic remagne- tization. Samples show only a present field magnetization or, at one locality in northwestern Alabama, a dual- polarity magnetization of probable Mississippian age. Rock magnetic studies indicate that higher concentrations of magnetite are present in the remagnetized rocks of the Nashville Dome and the overthrust belt than in the nonremagnetized Mississippian carbonates. We therefore conclude that magnetite authigenesis and remagnetization are related events in this setting and that the remagnetization must be due to chemical pro- cesses.
